utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the witness now? We will have the appearances first. MR.. NIEMANN: If your Honours please, my name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Ms. McHenry, Mr. Turone and Ms. Van Dusschoten for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have the appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Edina Residovic and I am appearing on behalf of Mr. Zejnil Delalic. My co-counsel is my colleague Eugene O'Sullivan, professor from Canada. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Zejnil Olujic, counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. Appearing on behalf of Mr. Mucic with me is my colleague Mr. Michael Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, I am Salih Karabdic from Sarajevo, appearing on behalf of Hazim Delic. My co-counsel is Mr. Thomas Moran from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your honours, my name is John Ackerman and I appear for Esad Landzo along with my co-counsel Cynthia McMurray. I would like to make a note at this point that today, Pakistan is celebrating its 50th anniversary of independence and I wanted to congratulate Judge Jan, and I know my other colleagues will join me in my congratulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Kindly tell the witness she is still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubac, may I remind you you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Ms. Residovic, continue with your cross-examination. Gordana Grubac (continued)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good morning, Mrs. Grubac. I hope that you have managed to rest a bit better since we are having a cooler spell, and the warnings that we mutually exchanged yesterday still apply today, so please be so kind to listen to the translation of our words. Mrs. Grubac, as your parents had a family house in Bradina, you probably know well the area of Bradina, is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you know that the hamlets in Bradina are on the slopes of a mountain, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that in the area there are very many isolated houses, family homes, which are isolated on the various hillocks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you can agree with me that after the fighting in Bradina when the men had mostly been taken away, that it was quite risky under such circumstances for families, especially women and children, to remain in such houses, can you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the houses in Bradina women could not remain because the houses had been burnt down, most of the houses had been burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Probably one of the reasons why -- that is probably one of the reasons why you as well as many other peoples tried to go down to Bradina to stay with relatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It is in that sense that I understood that you, together with the bestman at your wedding, Drago Pavlovic, went down to the city of Konjic three days later, and since you were unable to enter your flat you stayed for a month as a house guest, you and your children at the apartment of Mr. Drago Pavlovic, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was there but other women were unable to leave the school in which they had been locked up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, Mrs. Grubac, is it correct that the reason for your staying in the apartment of Drago Pavlovic in addition to the reasons which you have already adduced, was also the fact that he was living in the neighbour hood of Bozo Lokas, who was the uncle of Mr. Goran Lokas?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was one of the reasons, one of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew Goran Lokas who, before the war, was the presiding judge of the court and you heard at the time that he was also the chairman of the commission for the interrogation of detainees in Celebici; is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know that he was the chairman of that commission. I did know, however, that he had some role in the commission. I was not aware of exactly what role he had. I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubac, you wanted to establish contact with him as a friend, as well as a man who was influential, had some influence, because it was common knowledge probably at the time that Goran Lokas had helped release a number of prisoners from Celebici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew that Goran was in this commission and that he wanted to help Serbs in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, regrettably at that time you were unable to do that because Goran Lokas had been in a traffic accident and was no longer in Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I shall now ask you about some other things to which you have testified in court, namely you have said that you went to visit your husband a day prior to his release and that on your way back from Celebici, you and your sister-in-law missed the train which went between Jablanica and Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you, you know that when you got to Konjic a certain time after your arrival somewhere in the beginning of June, this train started -- the traffic of this train between Jablanica and Tarcin was resumed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It did run. I do not know when it started running. I know that it ran from Jablanica to Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You went to Celebici aboard that train?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that train was free of charge for all the passengers at the time, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And everyone who so wished, irrespective of ethnic background or any other affiliation, could ride on that train, could they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you also know that for the establishment of the operation of that train, Mr. Delalic had a prominent role to play in the reestablishment of the operation of that train and so that train was also dubbed a certain name, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. As you missed that train and there was no regular traffic you set out on foot, and as you have testified before this Tribunal, when you were passing by the house of Zejnil Delalic you saw a lot of soldiers there and dogs, and that reminded you that perhaps Zejnil Delalic could be at home. This is what you testified to, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that as you were friends in a certain way and also associated with his brother Sefik, you actually knew that at that time Zejnil Delalic was in Konjic only very seldom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is why you opted -- rather it occurred to you to make use of the fact that you knew that he was in Konjic at that time to give him a call?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I waited for Zejnil to come to Konjic because his brother talked me into it, into calling Zejnil once he came to Konjic and then I made use of that opportunity to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You have described in detail before this court the telephone conversation which you had conducted with Mr. Delalic and I have no further questions on that score, but I should like to ask you, on the basis of that conversation, did you gather that Zejnil wanted to help you, that he would help you if he could?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the basis of the conversation, I thought that he would help me to the effect that he would be released from prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Mrs. Grubac, so it was somewhere in the beginning of June that you came to Konjic again, and probably it was then when you came that you saw that Konjic, in the period in which you had been absent, which is to say from 7th May to the date of your arrival, had already been damaged from the shelling very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my arrival from Bradina I could not see that in the part of town in which I was there, there were no visible consequences of shelling and that was the beginning of June, and the section in which I was is the railway station area, and that part of the city is called Trsanica. That part of the city was damaged only very slightly at the time as far as I could see after coming from Bradina. This is at the very entrance to the town from the direction of Bradina, this Trsanica section of the city.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you what day it was you came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was 28th, I think, of May, three days after visiting Bradina, or perhaps in the beginning of June. In between that period, perhaps, from 28th May to beginning of June, I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, later while you stayed in Konjic you were also a witness of severe shelling of the city?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And on 4th June, it was precisely that quarter, that section, the department store and the area around there which was subjected to heavy shelling, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were shells landing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of that fact and everything which transpired, you could feel an anti-Serb mood gaining foothold in the city among the ordinary people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could feel that before that shelling also, even during the time when I was still working and towards the end of April when I went to work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You could also see for yourself that very many refugees from various parts of eastern Hercegovina, eastern Bosnia, had come to the city and the mix of the population had changed quite a lot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could see refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you noticed that even some friends of yours were averse to communicating with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not averse, they did not communicate with me at all. They just would not communicate with me at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But as you testified yesterday, there were people anyway, there were some individuals who had not changed their attitude towards you as acquaintances or friends.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three individuals, very few.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you knew that these people, because of that, were subjected to various harassment, to various gossip, even on the part of their own fellow citizens?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were with me only very infrequently, and in a very discreet fashion, shall I say. They were not all that conspicuous, you know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But precisely on account of that risk, of the danger because the milieu would then proclaim them to be fifth columnists, that is why?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the way I perceive it in respect of these particular people and I had no explanation as regards the others and their behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubac, you have said that after a number of attempts, somewhere around the second half of September, or perhaps if I calculate the days according to what you have said, perhaps after 20th September, you and your husband went to Mr. Delalic for a sitting, as we would put it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, it is also true that prior to that date you had also endeavoured to establish this second contact with Mr. Delalic, but at the time he was always somewhere in the war theatre, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not so. When we decided to pay a visit to Zejnil, that was only a day before that date, not earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That evening when you came to Mr. Zejnil Delalic's house, you were received as acquaintances and as friends, is that not so? His attitude towards you was the kind of attitude one has towards acquaintances and friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you stay there and engage in a normal conversation, friendly conversation, which lasted for almost four hours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have said before this Tribunal what the topics of your conversation were and what the actual cause for your visit was, so I shall not enquire about that. That is definitely in the transcript. You have also testified that Mr. Delalic immediately told you that it was very difficult, was very unlikely that he would be in a position to help you precisely in terms of what you were asking for, but he did propose first of all to your husband to come with me to Igman or to Tarcin if he was not feeling safe enough where he was; is that a fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said so, but we did not believe that he was unable to help us. We did not believe him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. You also said that he told you that he could possibly help you in regard to the return of your flat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did say that, but he did not help us. If I can explain a bit --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have explained to the court several days after that you were arrested and probably you never encountered Mr. Delalic any more after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Connected to that particular conversation, I still have one question. In the course of that talk, you found out that he had departed from view, to quite an extent, from many people, and you also saw the wanted warrant which he showed you in a newspaper. However, what I would like to know is: at a certain point when you were talking about how he could help you, he also offered you some funds and you said that you did not need it and you thanked him, declining the offer; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have clarified that your husband was again arrested in the beginning of October by the MUP and it is true that in the end of December Goran Blazovic, an officer of the HVO, released you this time from prison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He took us out of prison and ipso facto, I believe that he released us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you left the prison, you probably heard that Zejnil Delalic had left Konjic and then you certainly also heard, and perhaps also watched on television, a programme which was made by Sagolj with Jasmin Guska in which Zejnil was accused of collaborating with the KOS and escaping on a Chetnik helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know Zejnil left Konjic and he left it while we were still in prison. I heard this from the guards that were watching us. As far as this programme is concerned, I really do not know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubac, thank you very much. I believe that you have said in the sincerest of fashions what you knew about -- what you know about the events which are the subject of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: With your permission, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good morning, Mrs. Grubac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: For several days you have been in The Hague together with your husband, but I hope we will finish this by the end of the day. I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic, I have several questions to put to you and I would like to ask you to bear in mind the previous remarks made regarding the technical matters, that you also wait for my questions to be interpreted before giving your answers so that everyone in the courtroom can follow the proceedings. I hope we understand one another.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Grubac, tell me please, in the course of your direct examination you said that before the attacks started and before the unfortunate war occurred in the territory of the former state, that you were working in a bank; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you work anywhere else in the course of your career except the bank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the social accounting service of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So your career was always linked to banks, social accounting, banks and so on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When you left Konjic and Bradina, now that you have left that area, do you come across people from Bradina nowadays, people who were forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you meet people from Celebici camp, former detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you talk to them about your native area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course we do. That is what hurts us most.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Do you talk to them about the events from the past war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, that is the main topic of our conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Is anyone taking care of those people? Is there some kind of an Association of Detainees which concerns itself with the fate of the former detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is an association, but I do not know what you mean by caring for them. It does not give them financial aid, it has not found accommodation for them. It is just an association that the detainees collaborate with because of The Hague Tribunal, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What about the authorities? Do they care for them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No one cares for them any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can it be said that these people have been betrayed, in a sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what the word betrayal implies in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When no one takes care of them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They take care of themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubac, were you a member of the communist party or the League of Communists of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was, since the age of 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In the course of your testimony, you said with reference to Dr Hadzihuseinovic that he benefitted from his manifestation of extremist tendencies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that I said that. I do not know what you mean by "benefit".

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you ever think that he might gain from demonstrating extremist tendencies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I was surprised why he agreed to lead a nationalist party.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: He was the mayor, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And who was the mayor before him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly. I do not know. I know that Tomo Kures played an active role in politics and some other people, but to be frank, I really cannot tell you, I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubac, could it be said that due to everything that happened quite a number of Serbs lost their posts and property due to the war and the atrocities that occurred there; can that be said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Serbs lost everything with this war, their land ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Could you list a few of the most important people who lost their positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not the positions that count, it is human lives. They have lost their dearest ones, which is most important of all, and then after that they have lost everything, their identity -- I am sorry, I am a bit upset. They have lost everything, everything. We are people without a past.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You worked in a bank, in the social accounting service, this was a very significant position. You were a member of the communist party. Were you active in society, in politics before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, except for being a member of the party, I was not acting in politics at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You are familiar with Mr. Drago Peric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just knew him because his wife was my teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubac, who had the majority as an ethnic group in Konjic at the time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Muslims were in the majority. There were more than 50 per cent of them. I do not know the exact personal share, but I know they had more than 50 per cent of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief you said that you were from Bradina, that that is where your parents' house was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So you know Bradina well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could say that I do know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You said that all the houses in Bradina were burnt, is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the first attack, they were not all burnt down. Very few houses remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Could you list us the owners of the houses that were burnt down, if you can?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bradina is a large village and it is difficult to give you the names of all the owners of the houses. It is impossible. I can manage some names, but Djordjics, the Gligorevics, the Kuljanins.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When Bradina was attacked, is it true that there were about 3,000 attackers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard that later, I do not know the exact number, but they said there were about 3,000 of them. This was the story going round Konjic afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So you do not have direct knowledge, it is only what you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is only what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How many people were defending Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There may have been between 200 and 300 people, because there were no more men than that in all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did the defendants have military equipment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No uniforms, but they had some weapons, some rifles and things.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In addition to rifles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not tell you, I know of what I saw in my part of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You lived in Konjic before the war; your husband is a psychiatrist, so you were a person moving around in the Konjic society. You are a family that enjoys respect. Can you tell us the name of the JNA commander in Konjic until the JNA left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I really do not know. I was not active in politics and therefore did not consider it important to know who was the commander, so I really could not tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So you do not know who was the commander nor what ethnic group he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know at all who was the commander of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you know any officers in the Konjic garrison?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubac, could you please tell me, you know Mr. Zdravko Mucic, do you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Zdravko Mucic only by sight. We did not even greet each other when we saw each other in the street. That is how much we knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When did you have your first contact with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I contacted him for the first time in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How did he receive you, Mr. Mucic? Was he courteous, was he arrogant, was he ready to help you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can say that he was cordial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In the course of your direct examination, you said that Mr. Mucic said that Jusufbegovic was the one who had sent your husband to the camp; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In answer to my husband's question, "have you contacted Mr. Jusufbegovic" and Pavo intervened and said, "do you not know who it was who sent you to prison?" I think he implied Jusufbegovic and Rusmir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: From this contact you had with Mr. Mucic in the camp, do you believe that he had the power to release your husband himself, or did that depend on other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not think about that at the time, because I knew Pavo too superficially to be able to ask him to do something like that for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubac, can it be said that you have nothing bad to say about Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in the camp and he should have known that people were killed in the camp and he should have done something to help those people to prevent them being beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But judging from your own contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there is nothing bad I can say about those contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can it be said, Mrs. Grubac, that Mr. Delalic and Mr. Mucic and later other people who helped you, were, in a sense, ostracised because of this in their own environment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Pavo and Mr. Delalic did not do anything to help us, because Konjic as a whole was a camp for the Serbs. So the only assistance that anyone could give us was to help us get out of the town, and nobody did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What do you want to say when you say "Konjic was a camp"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me explain. My husband was under house arrest, even after his release from the camp. He could not move around anywhere. Secondly, whoever wanted to could arrest us, imprison us, give us nothing to eat. Nobody gave anything to the Serbs, and this is obvious from the fact that two days (sic) after my husband was released, we were captured again and held in prison for two months and my children were alone. My son who is 18, his hair is half grey, so I think that the only assistance that we would have wanted was to get out of that town.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So there was no great difference between Konjic and the camp at Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody beat them, but they were under house arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So you feel that Konjic, too, was a camp because of restricted freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could not even leave our houses -- not leave town, but we could not get out, could not go out. We were given I think to eat -- there was no institution to give the Serbs flour or food. If we did not have some money, we would have starved to death.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubac, do you know that Mr. Mucic advised your husband to leave Konjic and your husband refused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Grubac, can you confirm that the quieter ones that Mr. Mucic belonged to were against violence, and that as a result they were at risk in their own environments? This is similar to a question I have already put to you. What is your own personal impression? If you do not know, say that, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: If I may ask for clarification, I think there may have been a translation issue, and I just do not understand the question. The transcript says: "Can you confirm that the quieter ones that Mr. Mucic belonged to ..." I just would ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The quarter to which he belonged.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they did not prevent crime, and by not preventing it, my opinion is that they condoned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Grubac, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, again it is going to take a second to get me plugged in. May it please the court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask to go into private session for a couple of minutes. I want to talk about a subject that is rather delicate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: 13. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have no questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is there any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Just briefly, your Honour and I think it may have been a translation error. I did not know whether it would be better to interrupt or ask. Ma'am, at least the English translation of something you said in cross-examination, I believe to Mr. Olujic, said that two days after your husband was released from Celebici you and he were arrested again. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: She said that, but actually it was two months. Her husband was released at the end of July and re-arrested in October. She said two days but meant two months.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: When you were re-arrested, when your husband was re-arrested and you were arrested, were you brought to Celebici or somewhere else where you then stayed for several months?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to the MUP in Konjic, the police station in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCHENRY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: This is the end of your questioning. You are discharged. You can go. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think it is convenient for us to take the motion for protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: For the witness to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the motion we have filed in this matter, I just wish to make a correction and a clarification if I may in relation to the written motion before I make any oral submissions on the matter. Your Honours, firstly in paragraph 1, there is a reference to documents not being disclosed to the public and media. That is slightly imprecise in the way it is expressed there, your Honour. It should relate to if in the event of any photograph or sketch or some such matter in relation to the witness, should it ever be produced, that it not be released. It is fairly unlikely, I would imagine, that that would occur. Also in relation to paragraph 2 of the relief requested, on page 3 of the motion, your Honours, there is a reference there to image and voice altering devices. In fact, the relief requested is merely for image altering devices. There is no request by the Prosecution for voice altering devices in relation to this witness. Your Honours, I do not think it is necessary for me to ask to go into private session at this stage in relation to the application, but it could do at some stage in the course of it. If that occurs because of some matter that arises, I will seek your Honour's leave to do that, but simply the basis of the application is this, that the witness came to The Hague on the weekend of 10th August, which was last weekend, and soon after he arrived here he sought this measure of protection which is contained in the motion we have filed. The witness is not seeking any other restriction, the transcript -- he is not seeking any restriction in relation to that. He is not seeking any restriction in relation to his name or identity in that sense. It merely is the visual presentation of his face that he is concerned about. Your Honours, he has said that he is in a part of Bosnia at the moment where there is a movement of peoples back into the area, and he has a wife and child and he considers that him giving evidence of the matters that happened to him, circumstances that he was placed in in the Celebici camp may cause him or his wife to be placed in danger. Your Honours, these issues are very hard to assess, but I think it is true there is a great deal of instability in Bosnia-Herzegovina and particularly in certain parts of it at the moment, and the Prosecution certainly has the view that the fear that he has is real fear and is justified in the circumstances, particularly in relation to the part of Bosnia where he is. This witness is an important witness to the Prosecution case. He gives direct eyewitness testimony of matters which go to central parts of the Prosecution case and to specific counts in the indictment. There is no evidence to suggest that the witness is anything but a trustworthy witness; indeed that criteria which was set out in the five criteria in both the Tadic case, which was adopted also in the Blaskic case, is probably not of great relevance, having regard to the fact that this is not an application for anonymity. It is merely an application for the restriction on the level of publication. There is, as I mentioned, I think, yesterday, considerable constraints on the ability of the Tribunal to provide witness protection once they leave this Chamber. I repeat what I said in that respect in this regard, that the most powerful protection that can be awarded to a witness is in the Chamber itself, and once they leave the Chamber it diminishes at a rapid rate until they go back to the place where they came from. If one is to be afforded the maximum protection that one can get, it is in fact during the course of the evidence and while they are here in The Hague. Finally, your Honours, in relation to the criteria, the measure that is sought is the least restrictive measure in relation to publicity that is sought. When I say least restrictive, it does not entail any significant constraints on publication, merely the publication of the face. As was observed, your Honours, in other cases relating to this question, the notion of public hearing and a fair trial must be interpreted, in our submission, in the context of the rather unique object and purpose of this Tribunal, namely that it is operating in an environment where, unlike, for example, the Nuremberg Tribunal, there is no direct control over what can happen in the former Yugoslavia where the witnesses live. Because of that lack of control, which was not the case in relation to Nuremberg, the allied powers had control and could enforce their will. That is certainly not the case here. There is some measure of control, your Honours would no doubt observe with relation to the Dayton Agreement and the UNPROFOR but that, in our submission, is far short of anything that was available during the Nuremberg proceedings, and certainly it is a long, long way short of what happens with respect to courts in national jurisdictions where the court has at its disposal such matters as police forces and the like. In respect of that, your Honours, the measure sought in relation to this witness is, in our submission, the least restrictive that we could seek. It is, in our submission, justified and unless I can help your Honours with any other matter, it is our submission that it is appropriate in these circumstances to grant this measure of relief. As your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do the Defence have any views on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only concern that I would like to express is the indications are, and we still do not have the material to prove it yet, but we have been advised that the last witness who requested this identical protection, Mr. Sudar, had, prior to leaving to come here, given a full interview on Belgrade television which was run immediately after his testimony here. If this witness has done a similar thing and done a television interview with Belgrade television or someone else, then it begins to appear that coming here and requesting this kind of protection is a bit gimmicky and may be sort of a way to make themselves feel important, "I went there and I got protection because I was so important". If they are giving television interviews to Belgrade television before they come here, then there is not much need to give them even this level of protection, it would seem to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was just going to present the same argument. I can understand that every witness can refer to special circumstances and this court can provide protective measures, but yesterday Mr. Ackerman raised an important question at a private session, and I think that we must all bear in mind that when a witness goes back home he may be exposed to various risks there. However, in addition to these protective measures transforming this trial into a secret trial, there is also a danger that some witnesses, such as one who asked for protection here, only a day later appeared under his full name on Belgrade television. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all due respect for my learned colleague on the Prosecution, any comparisons with the Nuremberg trial and everything else, I think that the spirit of the statute and the rules of procedure and evidence require, above all else, that the trial should be public. For the trial to be public it also means that it should be fair. The introduction of this kind of element as to whether a witness will have protection or not, and then later on we learn that in the mass media he is granting interviews, is simply a way of undermining this honourable court. I would even go so far as to say that it shows lack of respect, to ask for protective measures in the courtroom, to engage the technical services to give such protective measures, and then to grant an interview on Belgrade television or anywhere else, could in fact be described as contempt of court, and that is why we are opposed to such a carte blanche approach. Certainly, yes, for protective measures when this is warranted, and, of course, we can check the real need for it, but we would be against it becoming the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence of Hazim Delic cannot accept the reasons given by the Prosecution in their motion. The return of refugees is one of the key provisions of the peace accords, and it is the duty of this Tribunal, too, to work for the maintenance of peace, as it was established by the security council in line with the provisions of Chapter 7 of the Charter. To claim that the implementation of the Dayton Accords, with respect to refugees has some effect especially in view of the very limited number of refugees that are going back, and it is quite obvious that he is living in Republika Srpska, where very few refugees have returned to, and to claim that he is running a risk going there I think is really ridiculing the peace process in itself, which would mean that the peace process, as such, is a source of danger, and I think that such arguments cannot be accepted and should be rejected.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Just if I might be heard for one second. There is one question that needs to be determined --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You do not deserve to be heard after Mr. Ackerman has spoken. You should have asked your lead counsel if you should do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: So I am not going to be allowed to ask the one question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I would prefer it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Did Sudar appear on Belgrade television after appearing before us and seeking protection? This makes the whole claim rather ridiculous.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not seen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Although I would say, just because one witness has abused the concession granted to him, it does not mean it should be denied to everyone else. This is a very serious question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It does, your Honour. I would indeed be very disappointed if that happened, but I find it surprising for it to be suggested by Mr. Olujic that it did happen, considering that we made enquiries of the Victims and Witnesses Unit; we were informed at the time that this matter went to air in Belgrade, the witness was still in The Hague and had not left, so it seems to us, your Honour, that allegations of contempt and others -- if it is correct he was still in The Hague at the time, is a very serious thing to say of the witness, but we are still pursuing our enquiries, because we want to find out what the facts are, rather than rely on innuendo, suggestion and rumour. Your Honours, it is possible that this witness gave an interview before he came to The Hague. That is in itself an unfortunate thing, it is not something we, the Prosecution, knew about. It is possible he gave an interview beforehand, which is what Mr. Ackerman has suggested, and that that was published afterwards. We will pursue the matter and we will find out. In relation to it, your Honours, you are quite right; it should not be that because one witness does something like that that all other witnesses should be punished as a consequence of it. Certainly so far as we are concerned, we do all we can to discourage this sort of thing, particularly after the events, because it does fly in the face of the court's order and it is most unfortunate. Of course, as your Honours have realised we have absolutely no control over it. If they do it when they go back there, whether or not it amounts to contempt, I would be very surprised. Your Honours, the issue about secret trials in my submission is really overstating the matter considerably. This is not a question of a secret trial. In most jurisdictions video links to the outside mass media are unheard of, but the court is open, people can come in here, sit in the gallery, listen to the case, listen to the evidence. The only thing they are prevented from seeing is the face. In my submission it is no different to any other public hearing; there is no restriction on the transcript or anything of the sort. To suggest secret trials really is going too far. A secret trial is if we shut the blinds down and nobody could see it and the transcript was restricted. That is not our submission. In my submission, that is a highly exaggerated suggestion. Your Honours, unless I can assist you with anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly, I think I failed a moment ago by being imprecise. What I was trying to suggest, and apparently failed, was that before the court makes a decision about the matter with regard to this witness, we at least enquire whether or not he has given such an interview prior to coming here. If he has then it does not make any sense to give him this protection. That is what I was trying to suggest, and apparently did not do it well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, I share Mr. John Ackerman's view, and it is a way of safeguarding whether such interviews have been made, so before such applications are brought, there should be an undertaking from any of these witnesses that they have not conducted themselves in that manner. So if they now do, that will amount to a contempt of the Tribunal. But otherwise, I do not think, in the circumstances of this application -- we find that the Prosecution did not know of it before now, it was definitely not possible for them to have circulated the application so that we can provide for these exigencies. In any event, what it is now asking this Trial Chamber to do is just to alter the image of the witness and nothing more. His voice will be heard as it is. Those who can recognise him by his voice will still do so, and his identity will only be obscured to that extent. I do not know how the Trial Chamber can enforce the third condition which you said, not taking his photograph while he is "in the precincts of the International Tribunal", because they would not have known about this order. This order is just being made, and whoever is freelance around here, and does not know about this order, might proceed to do so. That is a fairly difficult one for the Trial Chamber to safeguard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and I would imagine that any photographs taken thus far, or sketches drawn thus far, of course, the order does not apply so it would not operate in relation to that, and indeed, I would imagine that if your Honour's order were made in relation to paragraph 3 and was not known, it would be difficult as well, but I am really talking more in the precincts of the public gallery and in the Chamber itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Definitely in the Chamber we can prevent that, but outside, "in the precincts of the International Tribunal", that is not just in the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I understand, your Honour. In respect of that, we would be content to amend it to say, "in the Chamber of the International Tribunal", instead of the word "precincts", if that makes it more effective in terms of your Honours' powers to enforce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: In my view, it is safer to keep it within paragraph 2 as amended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That is the main thrust of our request, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: That is the only thing we can do. If we leave it to paragraph 2 then it covers it. If you ask me too, I do not share the view it is a secret trial, because if you can hear his voice clearly everywhere, there is no secrecy about what is happening. Thank you. We will grant the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Do check up whether he has already made a statement to the television.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will certainly do that, your Honour. Might I be excused to speak to the witness, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Please do. The Trial Chamber will now have a break and come back at 11.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just two matters, if I may. Firstly, dealing with the question of whether or not the witness for whom I have just made application for protective measures, Hristo Vukalo, has given interviews in the past; he tells me he has not given an interview in the past and he tells me he does not wish to give an interview in the future and he will not do so, about the testimony he is going to give. The second issue your Honours is that we have been investigating the question of whether Branko Sudar, the one that was the previous witness that had protective measures did in fact give an interview to Belgrade television, since it was raised by the Defence to us the other day. Not only did we ascertain as a consequence of our enquiries that he was here at the time and could not have done it then, but what we have now discovered, your Honours, we have been informed by at least one person who was watching Belgrade television, that there was indeed a programme where Branko Sudar appeared, as evidenced. It was in fact a take off the Tribunal's broadcast which went to some British television studio and was then sent to Belgrade that had the face distortion which was applied by the technicians in this Tribunal. So it was nothing more than an extract of his evidence in this court. We are still continuing with our enquiries in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Apart from that, apart from Mr. Vukalo's wish not to give any interviews, if you extract an undertaking from him that he would not, that is quite a different thing from his voluntary decision not to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I did ask him, your Honour, whether he would be prepared to give an undertaking not to do so and he told me that he would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: With the Sudar thing, it is a difficult thing to imagine why they would relay the network from a British television --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It comes from the Tribunal, your Honour, out through the outlets to British television apparently. Then it was transmitted to Belgrade and apparently what appeared on Belgrade television was exactly what appeared here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: His distorted image, not an interview he gave?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, a reproduction of what appeared in the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us continue with Mr. Vukalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honours please. I call Mr. Vukalo. Hristo Vukalo (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You can take your seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Risto Vukalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, I should inform you that the court has granted you certain protective measures in relation to the giving of your testimony in these proceedings, insofar as the image of your face by mechanical means has been distorted on the television as it is transmitted from the Tribunal. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, could you please give your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Bjelovcina, in the municipality of Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born on 29th March in 1964.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you receive your education?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I completed four grades of elementary school in the elementary school in Bjelovcina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you continue your education after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Then I completed the rest of the grades, up on the eighth grade of elementary school, in the town of Konjic, in a school which was called is Zuonimir Nono Belsa in Musala, and I completed secondary school also in Konjic, machine technical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At the machine technical school, were you given special training in any particular profession or trade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I became a mechanic to operate machine tools.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, did you do your military service with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I served my military service with the JNA as a person of limited capacity, and this was due to my heart surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you do your JNA training in the limited capacity? What year, can you recall, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I went to the army in 1984 in the month of November. I do not remember the exact date. I served, I completed my service in 1985 in December. It was a full service term.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, what is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Prior to 1992, were you in employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was your employment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked with a firm -- actually in a factory in Slovenia. It was a Serb firm from Vranje. It was called SZP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the main product produced by this firm? What did they do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked as a welder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Prior to 1992 where was your residence? Where did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just say this, I found employment in 1990 at Igman in Konjic, and I lived in Bjelovcina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you still working at Igman just prior to the outbreak of military activity of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you living just prior to the outbreak of military activity in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was living in Bjelovcina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you married then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I have a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have an any children at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was four years old at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sir, were you yourself engaged in any form of military activity in the months leading up to the commencement of military activity in 1992, in the early part of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Approximately when did you cease working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere in the beginning of April they told us to go, or perhaps it was in March. I am not quite sure. Actually, we were assigned to the so-called waiting list, saying that we were redundant, that there was no work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is the waiting list at the firm that you worked for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and not only I myself but many Serbs too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were you doing between the period when you stopped employment up until the commencement of military activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed at home, I worked the land.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you remember when it was that the military activity commenced in and around the area where you lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before my village was attacked some checkpoints had been erected on the approaches to the town of Konjic. They were set up by the Muslim and Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to give the Chamber an approximate month when these checkpoints were first established in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they were established exactly for the first time I do not know, but I do know that there were checkpoints in April, because I could not go to the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you recall what date it was when Bjelovcina itself was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was attacked on 20th May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you when Bjelovcina was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, with my father I was bringing the hay inside the barn, and approximately around 4.00 or 5.00 pm, in the afternoon, firing could be heard from the direction of the village of Donje Selo and Cerici, the villages of Donje Selo and Cerici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you heard this firing commence, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I left whatever I was doing. I entered the house and my father went in the direction of a meadow where we had sheep to drive them back to their barn. I did not know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from your father, was anyone else with you at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My wife and my child were in the house, my mother and my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As the firing and the military action intensified, did you then seek shelter anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, after some 40 minutes or so, firing started at my hamlet from the five houses -- of the five houses which were the household -- where the households all bear the surnames of Vukalo. We could hear the firing and the shooting at the houses and there was shooting at the houses from the direction of the hill of Lovno, and from the direction of the villages of Hasanovici and Balmis, some 200 to 300 metres away from my hamlet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were frightened, we were surprised. They shot at the yards, at the houses, the children, the women, the elderly and the sick. All were fleeing every which way, actually towards the forest which was some 200 to 300 metres away from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you yourself flee into the forest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, with my wife and child and my mother and brother, and the other neighbours, women and children from among these five households.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went into the forest, did you take any arms with you, weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have any arms or weapons in the house at the time of the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the forest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Then what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Early in the morning, I do not recall the exact hour, we returned to our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did that include your wife and child and your mother?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At that stage, did you see or know of anyone who was defending the village against the people that were attacking it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My neighbourhood, my hamlet was away from the other houses -- distanced from the other houses some 500 or 1,000 metres, up to 1 kilometre. I did not hear any shooting coming from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At this stage did you know who it was that was attacking the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they were shooting at the houses they were shrieking, singing, actually howling. It was clear to me that they were -- I could make out that they were saying some words like "Allah U Akbar".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From those words did you deduce who these people were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Muslims and Croats from the nearby villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. The village of Bjelovcina, can you tell us what the make-up of the population is in terms of ethnicity; that is your village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The village of Bjelovcina had some 50 to 60 households. Of these households, four perhaps were Muslim and six to seven Croat households. It was surrounded by eight or more Muslim and Croat villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the majority ethnic population of Bjelovcina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority in the village of Bjelovcina were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to observe what the village was being attacked with in terms of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They shot bursts from automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall whether any mortar or heavy artillery was being fired at the village at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, rifle grenades were being fired, and on the next day, which is to say on 21st May, I also heard shells, but they were not quite near. They were falling somewhere on the lower section of the village. In fact I heard two of them land.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you aware of whether or not the JNA or the army of the Republika Srpska was operational in the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before this began the JNA had military centres in Celebici; actually the military barracks was there, and then in Ljuta and Konjic and Zlatar, they were driven away, and in Celebici, the soldiers of the Yugoslav People's Army were captured. This is what I heard from my neighbours. They were taken, as I heard to Split, so that there was no Yugoslav People's Army there at the time. In the village there was no Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any other form of organised armed resistance to this attack that you were aware of at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You cannot talk about some organised resistance, there were 50 or 60 able bodied men there, not more than that, not many.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were they engaged in defending the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the part of the population of the village of Bjelovcina, I did not hear either then or later that they had put up any resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say that you returned to the village the next day, 21st May, after spending the night in the forest. What happened then, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we came to our house it was chaos. The doors were broken down, the windows had been torn down. Everything was upside down in the house and furniture was broken. It looked like a storm had swept through the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We then stayed in the house repairing things and putting things back in their places, somewhere around 9.00 in the morning on 21st May, we saw some 200 to 300 metres from the houses, in the hamlet, across the meadow called Lopata, we saw three or four soldiers running towards our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw this happen, did you decide to do something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they came to a distance of perhaps 150 metres away from us, they ran to it, to that point, they opened fire again at this hamlet of mine. Then we fled again in the direction of the forest with the women and children, the elderly, the infirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you reach a time when you actually went down to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers kept shooting and calling out. Who in his right mind dare approach them? There was no warning and they shot at you immediately. So I went down, I descended below a large rock, under a rock, and my wife and my child did not manage to get out of that forest. She and the child were taken and taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who took them away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This Muslim army, Muslim soldiers and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you then later taken away by the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we went down not knowing what to do. We went down to the Muslim village called Kralupi and a relative of mine, when we were about 200 metres from the village of Kralupi, this relative went to see his bestman, Vahid and Amir Dzalilovic, because we did not dare go in with the women and children, fearing that they would shoot at us from the village of Kralupi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then Amir came, Amir Dzalilovic and he took us in front of a house where there were a lot of soldiers, Muslims and Croats, some of whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then this Dzalilovic, Arif, took me and my brother, Cedo and Davor, to his home and my mother and the other women and the others, they stayed behind in front of some sort of a small command in Kralupi that they had, near Arif's house. Vahid Macic came and he used to work with me in Igman, he was armed wearing a camouflage uniform, and a young man from the village of Turija, a Croat whom I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Macic, was he with the Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was armed, but he was not with the Muslims. There were Muslim soldiers in this village of Kralupi, but somebody had probably reported to some higher level command that we had got there, that we had arrived in Kralupi and he was probably sent to take me there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to you when you went there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As soon as he came he cursed me, but he did not hit me. They took us to Vejsil Salilovic's house, me and my brother Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: At the time when you made Vahid Masic, were you or your brother or anyone in the group that you were with carrying any weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened next? What was the next thing to occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the way, Vahid Masic cursed, but he did not hit me or my brother. When we got to Vejsil Salilovic's house near the elementary school in Bjelovcina we saw a lot of armed men, soldiers, and as soon as they approached one of them hit my brother. I did not know this man. He fell and then they started beating him. They shouted "kill the Chetniks", then they started beating me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the people that were beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, while I was on the ground covered in blood, Redzo Balic from the village of Zukici took out a knife and he was shrieking, he wanted to cut my throat and he pressed it against my neck. Then another soldier, I do not know who he was, pulled him away, because he was kneeling on my chest. I did not faint, but I was badly beaten up. My nose was bleeding, there was blood coming out of my mouth. Then they took me, Smajic was there, I do not know his name but I know his nickname, he was known as Duda. They took me to a house 50 metres away, it is 50 metres from Vejsil's house to this one. The house was owned by Boza Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Smajic, was he a soldier or one of the people that had been captured?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in uniform, a Muslim with a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to you when you got to Tomic's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took me upstairs on the first floor of the house into the room where this Duda hit me again and he ordered me to lie down on the floor. He hit me with his rifle butt, he kicked me with his soldier's boots and with a stick made from a cable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What part of his body -- what part of your body was he hitting you on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was hitting me most on my back and all over the body, but most on my back and legs. Then later he found a broom. I was fainting in the meantime. When he found this broom, then he hit me with that too, and he was joined by a blond man, younger than me, I do not know his name. I know he was a Croat, and so the two of them hit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say you fainted. Did you faint or lose consciousness just the once or did that happen a number of times?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I fainted several times, but they poured water over me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When this happened, you were brought back to consciousness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from you, was anyone else being beaten at this time and at this place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was just me upstairs with these two people, Duda and this other Croat soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat me for about an hour in that room, and then they told me to go down to the cellar. I could not walk, because my legs would not hold me, they were so painful. So they pulled me down the steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "they", do you know who it was that pulled you down the steps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These torturers of mine, the people who had beaten me in the room, Duda and this soldier from Turija whose name I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got down to the cellar, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They threw me against a wall and I sat down. I saw the owner of the house there, Boza Tomic, who was also covered in blood. My brother was also there, and Vlado Vukalo, Milenko Vukalo. They did not beat me much there. They did slap us, one of the soldiers, I do not know which one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the next thing that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then they took us in the direction of the village of Pokojiste. I could not walk so this Croat soldier had to help me, and it is with his help that I somehow managed to reach Pokojiste. They took us to Branko Jozic's house, he was also known as Aga. They leant me up against a wall, also in a sitting position. I was leaned up against a wall and I saw many soldiers there, in uniform and armed, and among them I recognised some of my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to name some of the neighbours that you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised Ivica Kozaric, a Croat from that village; Niko Jozic, a Croat from that village; Branko Jozic, known as Aga, because the command there, I realised then, was situated in his house, this was a higher level command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: These people that you have just named, these Croats you just named, were they in uniform at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were in uniform and carrying rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once you arrived at this command centre, where were you then taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They did not hit me there, but two people sat next to me and hit me on the nose. They did curse me, and later a van appeared. They took my shoes off and they took me, my brother, Boza Tomic, Vlado Vukalo, Milenko Vukalo, to the motel in Konjic. I observed that there were very many soldiers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this at the motel where there were many soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Konjic motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these soldiers also in uniform and armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who it was that took you to the motel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the driver, I do not know the two armed soldiers -- I do not know what they were called. I just know they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you got to the motel where did they take you then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took the whole group, Vlado, my brother, Milenko, Boza Tomic and myself upstairs to a room, a room for guests before the war, it was a hotel room. They told us that we should rest there and two armed soldiers guarded us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Approximately what time was this in the day or night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was on 21st in the evening, just before dark fell -- no, it was already dark. I do not know what the time was. However, sleeping was out of the question. Every five minutes, these two would come in and hit us, kick us, they would curse at us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say these two, do you mean the two soldiers that were guarding you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am implying those two guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened the next morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning, I do not know what time it was, it was early, it had already dawned, they told us to go down, they would apparently give us some breakfast and coffee. We went down to the hall -- the dining room, actually. However, nothing came of breakfast and coffee. I saw there somebody from Celebici, Masic. I think his surname was Masic. I cannot recall his first name, known as Barba, that was his nickname. He was in uniform, and he took us into the kitchen one by one and beat us there. This fate befell me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they say anything to you when they took you into the kitchen and beat you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
