utterances.text: He would just call out, one by one, "into the kitchen", beat us up there and shove us back and then the next one's turn would come so that Vlado, Milenko, Boza, Branko and myself had the same treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the next thing to happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After that Duda arrived, the one I have already mentioned, and a boy from Zlaticevo, a soldier, I do not know his first or second name, and they took me alone upstairs, into a room upstairs. Here they started to hit me. They hit me all over my body, and I had already previously been beaten up. I could only just keep conscious, and then someone walked in, I think he was an officer of that Muslim army at the time. Later, I saw him when I was working in the town of Konjic, outside the command building, which was just in front of the Standard, across the way from the Standard. He asked me whether I had a wish. He behaved correctly, I am thinking of the officer, and he said -- and I said that I would like to see my wife and child if possible. For a moment he interrupted the beating and the torturing by my torturers. My wife came, after about 15 or 20 minutes. They brought her into the room where I was, bloodstained, lying on the bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did your wife do when she came into the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She cried.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did they do anything to your wife when she cried?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they said that she would suffer the same fate as I, that she was a Chetnik woman. However, only one of them slapped her, and this officer took her away, and I suppose they took her back to Musala, the sports hall, where my child and father were also imprisoned and some other women and children. That was a prison by then already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After your wife left, was anyone else brought into the room then, any other prisoners brought into the room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after that they brought in Slobodan Babic and Novica Ivkovic from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When they brought those two in, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Duda, whom I have already mentioned, and this soldier from Zlaticevo and some others started to hit us. They hit us all over, but mostly on the back. I fell between two beds, I fainted, and then they probably stopped hitting me. When I came to, being busy with the other two, Slobodan Babic and Novica Ivkovic, they were hitting them a lot, I raised myself to the bed -- actually, no, I must correct myself. I do not know how I got to the bed from the floor, somebody may have lifted me up. I was lying on the bed, anyway. I came to, and I saw well with my own eyes when Duda cut with his knife. I do not know whether it was his right or left hand, lower hand, below the elbow, he cut off a piece of flesh with a knife to Novica Ivkovic. Then he trampled on Slobodan Babic's chest. He broke his arm because he trampled on his arm too. Others hit him as well, and they took turns coming in and out. I do not even know who they were in the end. They were all wearing uniforms. Then Duda, with a rifle, pushed the barrel into Slobodan Babic's mouth and perforated his palate. He was covered in blood, and he could no longer speak. He was just gargling. This went on, I do not know exactly, I think until about 2.00 in the afternoon and then this officer came whom I had mentioned, saying he was more or less correct with us, because he did not hit us. He interrupted this torture. He was shoving the soldiers out, and he told us to go downstairs. Novica went on his two feet; I was helped by a soldier, whom I do not know, but I somehow managed to get back on my feet. I saw that Slobodan could not stand at all. Then Duda and another soldier dragged him down the stairs, and his head was hitting the steps. They were laughing while they did it, and making jokes about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in the motel, did anyone offer you or did you receive medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was going to say that, I forgot. Actually, this officer, when he managed to stop the beatings, asked we would like to see a doctor. Of course we needed a doctor. A lady doctor arrived who had worked in Konjic, in the hospital, before the war, and a male nurse, called Vinko Jozic, whom I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know the ethnic background of the doctor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the doctor, she was Muslim, and the male nurse was a Croat. When they came in, the two of them, into the room, the room appeared like a slaughterhouse. There was blood on the walls, on the beds, it looked awful. She said, referring to Slobodan Babic, that he was apparently drunk and that he had fallen and hurt himself, and she was laughing as she said it. She said that we did not need any assistance, though we were all covered in blood. However, I asked this male nurse to bandage my right -- I think it was my right, because I felt nothing in the elbow area, I thought it was broken. He said he dared not from the doctor, and when she walked out for a couple of minutes, she went out for a couple of minutes, she left the room, he did bandage my arm, or rather he tied it round my neck and he did not dare give any treatment to Slobodan. As for Novica where the flesh has been cut off by Duda, he quickly bandaged it before the doctor came back and then both of them left, the doctor and the nurse.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you taken from the motel to another place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got outside in front of the motel I saw Mirko Babic. He was black and blue from blows and there was blood on his head and they loaded me into a car that was parked in front of the motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say they, do you know who it was who loaded you into the car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the soldiers, but I do not know their names or surnames, they were in uniform. They were there in the motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you were loaded into the car, were you taken somewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I and Mirko Babic were taken to Celebici, and there they put us into number 22 where that camp had been founded. We were there in Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You say number 22, do you mean room number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hangar number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And Celebici is the former JNA camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was the former JNA barracks, a smaller barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were there many people in room 22 when you first arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I entered this hangar number 22, I found there, among those I knew, Veljko Babic from my village, and also the following people I will mention are from my village, Ranko Dordic, Scepo Vukalo, and about six or seven men from the village of Brjdani who had already been there five or ten days before, I do not know how many days before, but they were there when we arrived. So they were the first detainees of the Celebici camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe the interior of room 22 when you first arrived at the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was like a warehouse for fire extinguishers. There were quite a number of water hoses there, pumps used for firefighting equipment, there was quite a bit of that equipment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any bedding in room 22 when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no beds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any medical supplies that you could see when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand. Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am sorry. Did you see any medical equipment or medicines or things of that nature in room 22 when you first arrived there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand now. No, I did not see any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You have already mentioned quite a number of people that you saw in room 22. Are you able to estimate approximately how many people were detained there, in room 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived there, when I was brought in to 22, there were about 12 or 15 men. I do not know the exact number, but I think there were not more than 15, but later, they were brought in in groups. From my village, from the Donje Selo and from the village of Cerici, so that by nightfall, there were many of us there. There were so many that we could hardly stand inside in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you arrived at Celebici, did you see Slobodan Babic again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Afterwards, after I arrived, maybe two or three hours later, I do not know exactly, they brought in my brother Branko, Vlado, Milenko and Boza Tomic and Novica and Slobodan Babic. They took Slobodan Babic out -- they were carrying him because he could not stand on his feet and they threw him into number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did Slobodan Babic stay there, in room 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was there, I do not know for how many days, but not many. I do not know whether it was a day or two, I cannot remember how many days, and then he was taken, apparently to the 3rd March hospital, which was set up a couple of days before that. Actually it was an elementary school, 3rd March elementary school, as it was called in Konjic. Then they brought him back again, he was completely naked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say they brought him back, they brought him back to Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To number 22 they brought him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When they brought him back, how long did he stay in number 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not long, I do not know how many days. He was immobile. He was not there for long, I do not know how many days. Then they took him again, I think to the 3rd March, but I do not really know where they took him. I later learned that he had died there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from being in room 22 at Celebici when they brought him back naked, did you see him in any other place in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see him, except in number 22 in Celebici. While I was in Celebici I only saw him there in number 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in Celebici were you interrogated when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was interrogated, but before that I was beaten by this Smajic Duda that I have already mentioned and some others that I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were interrogated, who interrogated you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First interrogation was by Mirsad Subasic from the village of Idbar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you known him before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know what his occupation was before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that he worked something to do with the army, he was attached to the department for the military. I think he went to some sort of school of that kind, but where he worked exactly I do not know because I did not know him very well. I knew him by sight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he was interrogating you, what were the sort of questions that he was asking you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked me how I had got there, whether I knew whether there were any other able bodied men in my village of Bjelovcina, and where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you beaten during the course of this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mirsad Subasic treated me correctly. He did not beat me, nor did anyone else beat me while he was interrogating me, but later when they took me back the guards hit me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of the guards that hit you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they were the military police, because they had white belts, but I know that there were two of them. I think one was from Dzajici and some were from Idbar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What were you beaten with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They beat me with fists, with their legs, with truncheons, and rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long were you in room 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In hangar 22 I think I stayed for about 15 days. I do not know exactly, but around 15 days. Then I was transferred to hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time that you were in room 22, can you estimate approximately how many people were there, how many prisoners were being kept there when the maximum number of prisoners were in room 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At one point I think there were about 100 of us, maybe even more. There was not room to sit down, we were all standing, we could hardly all stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in room 22 did you on any occasion go to any part of the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they started bringing in people in large groups, the population from Bradina, men who were put up in number 6, in the hangar number 6, one day I was carrying some bread there to that hangar, because I was appointed to do that by the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will ask you what you saw when you went there when we return. Is this a convenient time, your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. We can stop here for lunch and come back at 2.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Remind the witness he is still on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Sir, may I remind you you are still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: As your Honour pleases. Mr. Vukalo, when you were in room 22, you said on one occasion you went over to hangar number 6 to take some bread over. What did you see when you went over to hangar 6 on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me just say that I did not enter the hangar, I was in front of the hangar and the door was open and I could see the part that one could see with the door open.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you see in there, from that point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could see people beaten up, some were bandaged. Practically all of the people I saw were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You said that you were first interrogated by a person by the name of Subasic. Were you then later interrogated by somebody else when you were in the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Celebici, while I stayed there, there were many interrogations. I was interrogated by Miro Stenek, and there was another one whose name I cannot remember. I think he worked in the court in Konjic, and I think that he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you beaten or mistreated in any way during the course of those interrogations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many interrogations, as I said, and at some of those we would also get beaten and when we were interrogated by Miro Stenek we were not beaten when we were being actually interrogated, but we were beaten before and after the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you ever interrogated by personnel who worked in the camp, as opposed to interrogators that came in from outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were interrogated by the guards. I was also interrogated by Hazim Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When were you interrogated by Hazim Delic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall the date exactly. Once I was called out, to get outside. I was in hangar number 6 then, and he interrogated me outside the hangar and I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who beat you during this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hazim Delic did, and Esad Landzo, called Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: With what were you beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hazim hit me with his favourite thing which he almost always had with him; that is a baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you recall now what part of the body you were hit on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Under the arms, the part of my body where the ribs are, on the ribs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Hazim Delic ask you any questions during the course of this interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He asked me about a certain sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you say to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no idea what to reply to him. I did not know what he was talking about. I said there was no sniper, there was not anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say anything else to you during the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He mostly hit me then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you known Hazim Delic before you went to Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had not, not in person, but I had seen him around town, the town of Konjic, and later I knew that it was him, the person I had seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know where he came from, what village or town he came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean where he was born?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was born in the village of Orahovica near Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what position he occupied when he was in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While he was in the camp he was the deputy commander of the camp and later he was the commander himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time you were in Celebici, did you see him in the camp very often or not often? Are you able to give us some idea?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him quite often while I was in Celebici. He would enter as many as three times a day and for a while he also spent the nights there. He slept in the command building where they had their quarters. He came frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you think you would recognise him again if you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that participating in the interview or the interrogation that you were subjected to was Mr. Landzo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landzo also interrogated us on his own with the guards, and he also took part in that particular interrogation when I was being interrogated by Delic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you know Landzo by a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Already then when I was interrogated by Delic, I knew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you seen Landzo before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not know him before Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him in -- how often did you see him in Celebici camp? Was it occasionally, often, rarely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Initially Zenga was not a guard at Celebici, but he was there, he was in the Celebici camp. Later he was also a guard. He spent a lot of his time in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you think that you would recognise him again if you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from those people that you have mentioned being camp personnel, was there anyone else in the camp that you knew or came to know in terms of the people in authority in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard, but I did not see, that Zejnil Delalic used to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Anyone else in the camp that you knew or saw? I am speaking mainly of people that you saw when you were there who were in positions of authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were the guards, I cannot say what positions people held.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to give the names of any of the guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something which is etched in my memory, and it is an unpleasant memory, regrettably, in addition to Zenga, Osman Dedic, Salko, I believe that he was from the town of Konjic, and I do not remember his surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You have given the name of the deputy commander, Mr. Delic. Do you know who the camp commander was when you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. The commander of the camp, the administrator there was Mucic, Zdravko Mucic, called Pavo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Pavo was his nickname, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know where he came from, what village or town he came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pavo, and I will call him by his nickname, if that is all right, was from Konjic. I do not know his exact address. I believe it was Polje Bijela.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know whether he worked in Konjic or whether he worked somewhere else, before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before I started working at the factory at Igman, he also worked at that same factory. Then he left for Vienna, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him in the camp occasionally, rarely or often?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw him in the camp, how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wore a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you think that you might recognise him again if you saw him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I certainly could.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in the camp did you see there a person who was being detained as a prisoner called Pero Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when I came to number 6 from number 22, namely after we were transferred from 22 to number 6, I saw Pero Mrkajic in a pitiful state, all beaten up, lying on some boxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you known him before the war, that is Pero Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw him lying on these boxes, do you know approximately how long he was kept on the boxes or how long he was lying on the boxes for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could not say, but not for long.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did there come a time when he was taken from there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there did. He was taken to number 22, where there had been established a ward, where I had been before myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So the use of room 22 had been changed to a medical type place, had it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, so they told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see Pero Mrkajic again after he had been taken to this ward, that is room 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, later, after I do not remember how much time, we found out that he had died; he had succumbed to his injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in the camp did you come to know a person by the name of Kuljanin with the nickname Corba?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him in number 6 in the hangar number 6 when we from number 22 came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see anything happen to him during the period of time that he was in the camp that comes to mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the Bairam holiday in 1992, he was taken out, his name was called out, he was taken out of the hangar. He was then beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see this beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I could hear him screaming.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who took him out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo took him out. Then he came inside the hangar and after a short while, I do not remember exactly how long, he called out his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "he called out his name", who called out his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Esad Landzo did. Then a rifle shot could be heard and later we heard that he was killed, executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you did not see this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see it with my own eyes, but some of the camp inmates had seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This person Kuljanin, about what age was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, perhaps he was several years my senior.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If you could just assist us by saying whether it was 30s or 40s or 50s? You do not need to be precise.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 30 years, perhaps of age.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what his ethnic group was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Serb from the village of Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were in the camp, did you also see there a person that you knew called Scepo Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Scepo Gotovac came from my village. Of course I knew him. He was brought to number 6. I do not remember the date, I believe that it was on the orders of Hazim Delic, because when he was brought there and placed in number 6, the hangar, Hazim Delic slapped his face and told him that he would take his revenge upon him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you hear this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of us heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was by the door. Yes, of course I did see it. It was inside, in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was taken out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who took him out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga called out his name, then we heard a scream. We heard him screaming for 30 or 45 minutes. Then they put him back in the hangar and several hours later his name was called out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who called his name out again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga did. He was holding something in his hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who was holding something in his hand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga was. He sort of stuck it into his neck and he pushed Scepo Gotovac outside. Then we heard a scream again, then Zenga came inside after perhaps half an hour or 40 minutes, and he ordered two of the detainees --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who ordered two of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga did -- to bring him, Scepo Gotovac inside. While he was outside for the second time, while he was being beaten outside for the second time, for a time we could hear him moaning and screaming, and at a certain point it stopped. We could no longer hear him screaming. Of the detainees, Novica went out and his brother Toso Brdzani and they brought Scepo Gotovac half dead inside. In the morning I saw that he was dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How do you know he was dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went out to go to the toilet and I saw him, he was not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate his age, Scepo Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an elderly man, perhaps he was born in 1929 or so, I am not sure. 1929 is his year of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what his ethnic background was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were in the camp did you come to know a person by the name of Bosko Samoukovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was this man in the camp in relation to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He sat in the direction of the door, next to the wall of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This was hangar number 6, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While he was in the camp did you see anything happen to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was beaten, both inside and outside the hangar. Zenga hit him with his rifle butt. He kicked him and he hit him with a stick.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to see this yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Inside we were able to see it and, of course, outside I could not see it. After that he was transferred to the so-called infirmary at number 22, and after some time, I do not know how much time elapsed, I cannot remember that, since he had two sons there, Nedeljko and Milan, they were informed that he had died, that he had succumbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him again after you had been taken away to room 22 yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us approximately what age group he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe in his 50s, between 50 and 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And his ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Serb, from the village of Bradina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know approximately what time during the period of time you were in the Celebici camp that this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was before we were registered by the International Red Cross. I think this was sometime in June or the beginning of July. I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again, while you were in the camp, did you come to know a person that had a nickname, Keljo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had you known him before the war or known of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know him before the war, but I knew that he had a cafe in town but I did not know him before the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you come to know him in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was brought in later, after I had got to hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he brought to hangar number 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to number 6, that is where I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long was he in the camp for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly how long it was, maybe a month or two, I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did something happen to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. One evening, a friend of his came, a Muslim. He brought him some cigarettes. We could hear, all of us in the hangar, at least those who were closer to him, Hazim Delic said to this friend of him, Keljo's friend, I mean, "why are you giving him that? He will not see the day tomorrow", and he did not, in fact. In the early morning, he was called out --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who called him out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really could not say. One of the guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened when he was taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you hear this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some of the detainees were outside at the time, they were cleaning up. He was killed by Padalovic, as I was informed later, or rather as we in the hangar heard later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After he had been shot did you have to do anything in relation to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. After maybe an hour I was called out by Esad Landzo, known as Zenga, and he took me behind the hangar holding in his hand a grenade. He said to me that I had to remove the ring from Keljo's hand. How come he had that ring, I do not know myself. I was terrified, and he said that if I did not do it he would kill me with this grenade. I approached the body. I really do not know now how I managed to take off that ring. In that fear I somehow did, but before that I was having a hard time doing it and he said if I did not succeed I would have to cut off his finger. I gave him that ring as I did manage to take it off, and he said to me that I must not tell anyone because he would kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were taking the ring off Keljo's finger did he appear to you to be dead or alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again while you were in the camp did you see there a person that you knew by the name of Zeljko Cecez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew Zeljko before I came to the camp. He was from Donje Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war, his nickname was Spanac, or "the Spaniard". That is how his neighbours called him, in the 1980s and in the 1970s. How he came to the nicknamed thus I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what approximate age he was or what age group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zeljko may have been about 28. I think he was born in 1961 or 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know what his ethnic background was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was he located in the camp while you were there, in what place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He sat behind my back in number 6, the row behind my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the time that you were in the Celebici camp in hangar number 6, did you see something happen to Zeljko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Also during that holiday, ^ Kurban Bairam, the first or second night, I think it was the second or the first, I am not sure. He was called out by Zenga. One could hear moans outside, this was in the evening. The cries could be heard, I do not know for how long. Then the doors of the hangar opened and he fell inside like a sack. Zenga was still hitting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was he hitting him with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was kicking him, and I do not know exactly, I think he had a plank. He was crawling, he was going on all fours to reach his position. However, his strength caved in and he fell. We did not dare move any one of us to help him reach his place. When Zenga went out and when the door was closed behind him, I do not know exactly who it was who got up and dragged him to his place. In the morning, he was dead. He was lying there dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see him in the morning, see his body in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was it about what you saw of his body that made you think he was dead?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people who were sitting right next to him on his left and his right gave us the sign that it was all over for him, that he had died and one could see by his face, though it was all beaten up, it was yellow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again while in the camp, did you come to know a person with the name Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Milosevic is someone I did not know before the camp. I only know that he came from the village of Dzepi and I learned that in the camp. That is where I met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see anything or hear anything happening to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know Milosevic was beaten very badly, both inside and out. He was beaten by Delic also, and he died from the beatings, but I cannot describe that in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Again during the period of time that you were in hangar number 6, do you recall an incident where some prisoners were playing cards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did this incident happen, approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly, but I think it was towards the end of August or perhaps in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Some detainees had made some cardboard cards so as to while away the time somehow. However, no one asked the deputy commander of the camp, Delic, but one of the guards saw this and informed Delic. Delic came shortly after that and he beat us up en masse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you say "beat us up", just the people playing cards or other people as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those who were playing and those who had made them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you in this group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because I was playing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did this beating go on for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it only Delic that beat you, Hazim Delic, or was there somebody else there beating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were other guards too, but mostly Hazim was the one who hit us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he say anything to you while he was beating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he just said "turn around to face the wall of the hangar" and then he would beat us, and then he would go on to the next one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall what it was that you were being beaten with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that occasion when we had been playing those cards which we had made, he hit us with a spade, so that we had to spread our legs apart and our arms apart, and stand there facing the wall of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On what part of your body were you hit, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From our knees upwards, on our thighs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see an incident when you were in hangar number 6 where people were burnt with hot knives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw this happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw (redacted) when he was first called out, and then after some time he was brought back in. He had a terrible expression on his face. One could see that he was in terrible pain and he showed us his hands, and one could see the markings of a knife. The skin was all burnt, and then he told us both he and the other people who were taken out on that occasion, that Zenga had heated a knife until it was red hot, and then they had to hold it in their hands, and this, of course, would burn their skin on their palms. This was on their palms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned one occasion when a group of prisoners were beaten when playing cards. Were there other occasions when a whole group of people were beaten?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There were several such massive beatings, beatings of large groups, and there were occasions when each and every detainee was beaten. We called these "massive beatings".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where did these take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who participated in these beatings? Who was the one that was carrying out the beatings? Can you name some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember when the International Red Cross had registered us and some of the detainees tried to tell them of the situation we were in. However, afterwards, while the International Red Cross had still not even left, certainly they had not left Celebici, I do not know whether they had left the camp itself, Delic walked in with about 12 or 13 guards. He ordered us all to put our hands behind our heads and then they went round kicking us in the ribs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from kicking you in the ribs did they hit you with anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now and then one of them would hit us with a rifle butt. I also remember another such mass beating when some Muslim soldiers fell into an ambush made by their own people between Bradina and Repovci, so they all got killed in that ambush. Delic together with some other guards beat us, virtually all the detainees, and especially those from the village of Bradina. He beat us with his fists, with his boots. Sometimes he would give us a karate blow. This was the case with Ranko Gligorevic, known as Buco.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident were you were burnt with a fuse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly the date when this happened. Zenga, on that day, had done this to someone else before me. He tied the slow burning fuse, we call it the cord, round the naked bodies of detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see this happen yourself, did you see this happen to these other men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was done to me, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am asking you, did you see it happen to the other men ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was inside, in the hangar. I was called out also by name. I was told to get up. He tied this fuse between my legs, on my naked skin, and I had to take off my pants and my sweat suit that I had on, up to my knees. One end was inside, and then on top of that I would put on my pants and my jogging suit and the other end was free, outside. He would tie my hands behind my back, and then he would set light to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say you had to strip down, did you have to strip down to your naked body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my waist to my knees I was naked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was the fuse wrapped around your body or just -- perhaps you could describe. Where was the fuse wrapped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The fuse was wrapped between my legs and then one end would stay in my pants, in my particular case it was right next to the body below my underwear and the other end was outside, free.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Once the fuse had been put next to your naked skin, did you then have to pull up your underwear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and then he would tie my hands behind my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is this what you saw happen to the other prisoners?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, before me it was done to Vukasin Mrkajic, I think Veseljko Djordjic or his brother and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to them that you could see before something happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he did all this, when he wrapped the fuse like this and when they put on their pants and underwear and tie their hands behind their back and set light to it, then people were in great pain. They were almost jumping around half a metre high, making leaps into the air from the pain when the fuse started burning right next to the skin. They would roll over on the concrete floor until somehow they would manage to put it out with their own body. They would extinguish it rolling around like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was Zenga on his own when he was doing this or was he with other guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Osman Dedic was with him most times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Would he say anything or do anything while this was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would laugh, he would laugh. To him, it seemed very funny.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then he called me by name and told me to get up. He ordered me to take off my sweat suit up to my knees and my underwear, then he also tied this fuse round my body and ordered me to put back on my underwear and my sweat suit, to put my hands behind my back. The end of the fuse, which was uncovered, it was about 10 centimetres long, this uncovered end, and when he set light to it, because I had seen this happen to others before me, I saw that the best thing to do was to lie down as soon as possible and roll around to put the fire out, and I managed, before it reached my skin, to extinguish the fuse, but he did not like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "he did not like it", who did not like it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga. He hit me with his rifle, with the butt of his rifle. He sent me back to my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there another incident when a bullet was shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot precisely recall the exact time, the date. There were many beatings, very many unpleasant incidents and situations, but I think that it was some time around August, in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe this incident for us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He called me out --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who called you out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga did. He told me to go out and he himself was out, outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you say "out", that is outside the hangar, is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. What I am about to describe, he did, before he did it to me, to Vukasin Mrkajic, Bosko Samoukovic, (redacted) (redacted), as well as to some others, and when Vukasin Mrkajic was the object of this and he did the same thing as I am about to tell you he did to me, when he was doing that to him, what he was to do to me later, he told Vukasin Mrkajic to call me out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you did not see what happened to the other men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I later heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just tell us what happened to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I went out, I walked up to him, to a distance of some five metres from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: This is as you walked up to Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I mean Zenga. He told me to kneel. He ordered me to kneel, and I did. He showed me this bullet. He asked me, "what is this?", and I said, "it is a bullet". Then he showed me his rifle and he asked me what that was, and I said "rifle". I saw with my own eyes him put a bullet into the rifle barrel and cock. He told me to open my mouth wide. He approached me. I opened my mouth wide. I thought that my pain would be over and that would be the end. He shot. I did not know whether I was dead or alive. I could only feel some sort of a fire burning inside my mouth. It took me a minute to come to and to realise, to see whether I was alive at all. He was laughing and then he sent me back to the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What do you think actually happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later we found out from the other guards there that he actually took out the powder, somehow had emptied the powder, the charge from the bullet, so that actually the bullet could not be activated when it was being shot. It would just burn you inside, singe the inside of your mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall another incident that happened in the canal where the prisoners used to urinate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this appeared, as I mentioned before that they were ambushed by their own Muslim soldiers, so they fell into this ambush which had been staged by their own people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You do not need to repeat that. Just tell us the incident, if you would.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. In the morning as we were going out to urinate, we would go in groups of about 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this the sort of standard procedure, to go out each morning to urinate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at the time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where would you urinate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just to the left-hand side of the door, there was this sort of a ditch, canal, which was some 10 or 15 metres away from hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: On this particular occasion what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the door was opened we heard some sort of a racket in front of the hangar, and as soon as the door was opened Zenga started hitting some people and was telling them to approach him, and I later heard that after this first group had -- that is what I heard after this first group had returned from the urination. We were scared, we did not know what was going on. We did not know what was happening. So when this group, in which I also was, this group of 10 people went out to urinate, Zenga called me, told me to come to him, and I walked up to him and he hit me two or three times, and at a point which was some 2 metres from the last man on the right side in the line of men who were urinating, he ordered me to drink urine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: From where were you to drink this urine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the canal into which the others were urinating at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The men were urinating at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this group with which I had gone out to urinate, and he also pressed my head and he pushed my head down. He hit me very strongly with his rifle butt on the back, and he pushed my head down into the canal so that the urine was in my mouth and I actually drank it. He held me in that position until I could no longer endure it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you lying down with your head in the canal or were you kneeling down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was kneeling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How was he holding your head down into the canal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He actually pressed the back of my head, the rifle butt against the back of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the urine cover your face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my head was immersed in the urine; my head, my face, my mouth, my nose.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you actually take the urine into your body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall another incident when prisoners were forced to eat grass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe what happened on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will describe what happened to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga called me out. There were some other guards there, I believe that Zeba Cosic from the Muslim village of Idbar was also there. There they started to hit me and they ordered me to eat grass, to pluck the grass, so I grazed and I swallowed. I was subjected to the same treatment later by this guard from Idbar several times, on several occasions and Zenga did not force me to graze again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So what you are saying is, it was only one occasion when Zenga forced you to eat the grass?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident seeing something happen when a prisoner was forced to drink large quantities of alcohol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This was Vukasin Mrkajic. We would be taken out and this was done by Hazim Delic. He would order us out in front of hangar number 6, and we had to sit on the concrete in rows. We would have to strip naked to the waist, and then on one occasion after having taken us out and ordered us to sit thus, he brought for Vukasin Mrkajic a bottle, a cognac bottle, and told him to gulp it down over a very short period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who told him to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Delic did. Then Vukasin Mrkajic had to. Then he had to imitate the driving of a car, a car riding in terms of sounds that a car made and also to present the picture of a car being driven around. The guards and Delic found this very amusing and funny and they laughed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: While you were in the camp did you know of two brothers who were prisoners there by the name Dordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in the camp. I had not known them before I came to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where were they in the camp so that you came to know them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were brought later. They were brought later than the day to when I was brought to hangar number 6. I believe they were brought when this incident took place, the one involving Muslim soldiers who were ambushed by their own people and who were killed on that occasion. I believe it was on that day, but I am not quite sure. They were brought and they were put on the right side from the door, inside, in the camp --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In the same hangar as you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in 6, in number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you see something happen to these people, these two men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did. I saw them being hit frequently, hit hard. On one occasion, Zenga ordered one of the two -- actually forced one of the two to perform oral sex, fellatio. He ordered one of them to strip bare, down to his knees, and the other one had to hold his genitals in the mouth to perform fellatio.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you able to see this from where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he actually take the other man's genitals into his mouth from what you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One of the brothers had to put the other brother's member in his mouth, because Zenga threatened that he would kill them both unless he did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Had Zenga beaten them prior to forcing them to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from Zenga, were any of the other guards there at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Osman Dedic, of those that were inside. I do not know who was outside. They laughed at the scene and we could hear voices coming from outside as well, from in front of the door. We could hear laughter actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from these incidents, were prisoners ever forced to sing songs or say prayers? Did incidents like that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not sing, but I heard from the detainees that some did sing. On one occasion Delic took us out in front of number 6 and ordered us to sit down on the concrete. From the town of Konjic then came a wealthy man by the name of Smajic, whose nickname was Kurecen, and Delic ordered us to utter, to say "Allah U Akbar". He would ask, he would say, Delic, "who is the greatest?" We would say "Allah" once, and the other time Kurecen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long did this go on for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This went on for some 20 minutes or half an hour, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did it only happen on the one occasion, so far as you are concerned, or did it happen more than once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It only happened once, at least as far as I myself am concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall an occasion when the International Committee of the Red Cross visited the Celebici camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did they come to the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came, we had been registered. We were registered on 12th August 1992. This was the first time when they came to visit the camp in Celebici. There was Mr. Michel, I believe he was French. He was the head of this team that visited Celebici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from registering the prisoners, did they do anything else while they were there that you could see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did. During one visit of theirs, when they came as we were going out to urinate, Mr. Michel had a stopwatch in his hand and he stood by the door and he measured the time during which we were to perform it all. I believe that the time was around two minutes per group of 20 inmates. I know that he waved his head, but nothing changed for the better after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the Red Cross come back again after the initial visits?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were there then, and after they had registered us, they left -- he left. They came later again after a certain period of time. I do not know after how long, but two months must have elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I am going to ask you, if you would, to describe for the court some of the conditions that prevailed in the camp during the period of time you were there. Firstly, can you tell their Honours the toilet facilities that were available to the inmates in the camp during that time? You have given some description, I think, in your evidence of the place where you had to urinate, but can you give the Chamber some more details of what facilities were provided for you in relation to toilets?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will describe these conditions for you. While I was in number 22 we would go out to go to the toilet, which was outside. This was the procedure; we had to put caps, pull down caps on our heads and then we would go to the toilet thus, and on our way to the toilet and on our way back they would hit us. They gave this sort of a cap, the guards gave us a cap. Where they got it from I do not know. Each one of us had to put this cap on his head so that they would not be recognised, that we would not be recognised when we were being beaten. After some time, we did not use this cap any longer. The conditions in number 6 were horrendous. We lay in hangar number 6 on the concrete floor, and I slept on the bare concrete floor for some two or three months. There were no baths in the beginning at all. We were not allowed any visits. No one could come to bring us a fresh change of underwear. For a toilet, we used some kind of a bucket which was inside the hangar, it stood by the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was there any privacy provided for the toilet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the toilet have any sort of screen around it so you could have some privacy when you were going to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, none at all, just a metre or two from this bucket were the other inmates, the other detainees who were accommodated to the right from the door. Also to the left from the door there were also detainees. We used this bucket most often at night when we would be shut up, locked up. In the day, we did not dare be found there by any of the guards; that is to say when the guards came in or when Delic came in. We had to sit in our respective places. There was a foul stench and we also had our meals in that same place. It was very dusty, filthy. The people were infested with lice and I myself also had lice. The conditions were appalling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where you sat in your place, did they give you anything at all to sit on, or did you sit straight on to the concrete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the first two months I sit on the bare concrete. Later we were allowed to have a blanket each; we were allowed that our people could bring us a blanket each from our home, so I got a blanket and later I sat on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were you at any stage offered medical treatment while you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While I was in the camp, in number 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was beaten many times and never was any medical assistance extended to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the food and water supplied to you like? Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The food was horrible. For a time, we only received a loaf of bread for 17 detainees. One loaf had to be shared between 17 detainees, without any vegetables. Then later we would get some cooked food, some vegetables. We went to eat in groups of five, right there next to the door where the bucket which I described was. That bucket would be taken out during the day. One detainee could have four or five spoonfuls of rice, mostly it was rice, sometimes it was too salty, sometimes it was not salty enough, but the main thing is it was never sufficient. It was not enough in terms of quantity, and we all used five spoons, and we ate in groups of five.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Niemann. I think we will break now and come back at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. You may proceed, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Sir, when you were in the Celebici camp, did you know a person who was also a prisoner in the camp by the name of Damir Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Damir Gotovac? Yes, I did know him before the war because he is from my village of Bjelovcina, but he lived in Celebici for a time and he was born in Bjelovcina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When he was in the camp, was he kept in the same hangar as yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was in hangar number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident which involved both you and Damir Gotovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion he was taken out, his name was called out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who called him out, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zenga. One heard a cry, and maybe about ten minutes later one of the guards, I do not now recall which, called me out as well. I saw Damir there, Zenga was hitting him and he fainted and fell to the ground. Then Zenga told me to kill him, I mean to beat him to death. I said I could not do that. Let him kill me. Then they started hitting me, Zenga was there, and I think Osman Dedic as well. They started hitting me and then they ordered Damir to kill me. He refused, he said he could not do it. Then they beat both of us. I do not know how long this lasted. It was not for long, maybe half a hour, and then they sent us back into the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you saw Damir when you went out there and he had been beaten, was he wearing anything that you can recall on his head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he had a protective mask, military mask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did that cover his face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this mask was on his head. It was a gas mask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier in your evidence that you saw the camp commander, Mr. Mucic, come to the camp on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Zdravko Mucic is somebody I did not know from before, but the first night I spent in Celebici in the camp in number 22, Pavo came with, I think, Pero Serbia, as he was called, came with him. I learnt that later from the other detainees. He came through the door of room 22, and he said that he was the camp commander or head of the camp. I was standing near the door and the man who was with him was pushing us. Pavo said that we stank, that we smelled bad. He looked us over. I do not remember whether he spoke to anyone, but he left soon afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You have also said in your evidence that when you first arrived at the Celebici camp you were in room number 22 and you then went to hangar number 6. Did you stay in hangar number 6 for the entire period or the balance of the period that you were in Celebici, or did you go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, from hangar number 6 when a large number of detainees were transferred to the sports hall in Musala, there were 32 of us left, 32 detainees, who were transferred to room 22 where I had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When did you ultimately leave the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 9th December we were transferred to the sports hall in Konjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did Mr. Landzo stay at the camp for the whole time that you were there, or did he leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a period of time, I do not know exactly from which date until which date, he was not at the camp in Celebici, but this was a short period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the circumstances of how it is that he came to leave the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly, but I heard that --

utterances.speaker: MS. MCMURREY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am going to object as to his personal knowledge. We do not know where he heard this from. I know my learned colleague Mr. Niemann knows he needs to lay the proper basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will not press it. Just tell us what you yourself know. Was Mr. Mucic at the camp for the whole period of time you were there, that is the Celebici camp, or did he leave at some stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zdravko Mucic, known as Pavo, would come by occasionally. Sometimes he would not be there for as long as ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: After you left Celebici camp, where were you taken then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Celebici, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was taken to the sports hall at the Musala prison in Konjic, with the 32 detainees, the last remaining group of detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of the Musala facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I arrived at Musala, at that time I am not quite sure, but I think somebody called Broceta, but I do not know his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did he remain the commander of that camp or facility, or did the command change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During our stay at the sports hall in Konjic quite a number of the prison administrators changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Among the prison population in Musala, I mean the people who were being detained, I should say, were any of the former guards from Celebici there being detained along with the other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us who they were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A guard who was in Celebici, Kemo -- I think his name was Mrndzic, for a time he was in charge of the camp in Konjic. In Celebici, he beat us, but in Konjic, he was a good commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Anyone else that you can think of that was also being detained in Musala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand. What do you mean, detained?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Imprisoned there, kept there as a prisoner. Any of the former personnel from Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand now. For a time Esad Landzo was imprisoned there, Hazim Delic, who had been at Celebici, and they were also prisoners in Konjic at Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When Hazim Delic was also being detained as a prisoner in Musala, did you have a conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time we were upstairs in a part of the building that was known as the gym. He could come up whenever he wanted. He came during the daytime. He did not talk to me but he spoke to some other detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you hear the conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He would come in and once --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I only want you to tell us if you actually heard him speak yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On one occasion, I cannot recall exactly who he was talking to, one of the detainees, he said that the data about all the victims from Celebici, when they were born, what village they came from, even how old they were -- I can say that much, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During the period of time that you were detained in Musala camp, was there any mistreatment to the prisoners occurring that you could observe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for a time when Edo Zilic was in charge of the camp, or the prison rather, ten of us, and I was one of them, were told to go do some labour --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I will not ask you to go into details, I just wanted you to say yes or no, whether it occurred -- whether there was any mistreatment while you were in the Musala camp, but I will not ask you to give details of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was less, but there was some. Less, much less.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: The order in which you have agreed to take the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. First counsel for Mr. Delalic, second counsel for Mr. Mucic, third counsel for Mr. Delic and fourth counsel for Mr. Landzo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Vukalo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Edina Residovic, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. I would like to ask you, Mr. Vukalo, to wait to hear the interpretation of my question, the interpretation into English, and when the interpretation is over to answer my question, because in that way everyone can follow what we are saying. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vukalo, in the course of your examination-in-chief by the Prosecutor you provided the basic data about yourself. We know that you came from Konjic, that before the war you were working at the Igman factory until you were laid off just before the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukalo, I would like to know whether you became a member of the SDS immediately after it was founded in the municipality of Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the SDS party was founded, and the SDA party, the HDZ party, I did not immediately join, but on one occasion a man from the village of Bjelovcina who was a drunkard, actually, I do not know how that came about, but he joined the party and he picked up some membership cards. Then he distributed those cards in the village. Of course, he asked for some money for these cards, and that is how in my village, people joined that party, so that it was really not very serious.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore in 1992, before the outbreak of the conflict in the territory of the Konjic municipality, Mr. Vukalo, you became a member of the SDS in that way, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
